cards.question: What problem did the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017, 'Attention Is All You Need') aim to solve?
cards.answer: It replaced recurrent and convolutional sequence models with attention-only architecture, enabling parallel processing of sequence tokens and better modeling of long-range dependencies.

cards.question: What is self-attention?
cards.answer: Self-attention lets each token in a sequence compute a weighted combination of all tokens' representations, with weights determined by pairwise compatibility. This allows each position to gather context from any other position.

cards.question: Write the formula for scaled dot-product attention.
cards.answer: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V. Queries are compared to keys to get weights, which are then used to average the values.

cards.question: Why are the dot products divided by √d_k in attention?
cards.answer: For large d_k, dot products grow in magnitude and push softmax into regions with extremely small gradients. Scaling by √d_k keeps the variance near 1 and stabilizes training.

cards.question: What are queries, keys, and values?
cards.answer: They are linear projections of the input embeddings (Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V). A query asks 'what am I looking for', keys indicate 'what I contain', and values hold the information that is actually passed on.

cards.question: What is multi-head attention and why is it used?
cards.answer: It runs several attention operations in parallel with different learned projections, then concatenates the outputs and applies a linear projection. This lets the model attend to different types of relationships or subspaces simultaneously.

cards.question: Why do Transformers need positional encodings?
cards.answer: Self-attention is permutation-invariant and has no inherent notion of order. Positional encodings (sinusoidal or learned) are added to the token embeddings to inject information about token position.

cards.question: What are the main components of a Transformer encoder layer?
cards.answer: Each layer has a multi-head self-attention sublayer followed by a position-wise feed-forward network. Each sublayer is wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization.

cards.question: How does the decoder differ from the encoder?
cards.answer: The decoder has masked self-attention (preventing attention to future tokens), plus cross-attention over the encoder outputs, plus a feed-forward network. This preserves autoregressive generation.

cards.question: What is causal (look-ahead) masking?
cards.answer: A mask sets attention scores for future positions to -∞ before the softmax, so their weights become zero. Each token can therefore only attend to itself and earlier tokens during training and generation.

cards.question: What role do residual connections and layer normalization play?
cards.answer: Residual connections let gradients flow through deep stacks and ease optimization, while layer normalization stabilizes activations. Together they make training deep Transformers feasible.

cards.question: What is the computational complexity of self-attention, and what is its main limitation?
cards.answer: Self-attention costs O(n²·d) time and O(n²) memory in sequence length n, since every token attends to every other. This makes very long contexts expensive and motivates efficient variants like sparse or linear attention and FlashAttention.
